label: Yehezkel (Ezekiel) — Part 5 — Chapters 33–39
summary_plain: YHWH appoints Yehezkel as watchman: if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not warn the people, their blood is on his hands. YHWH declares: I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked — turn back, turn back from your evil ways — why will you die, house of Yisra'EL? YHWH denounces the shepherds of Yisra'EL who feed themselves instead of the flock — I will rescue my sheep from their mouths. YHWH himself will be their shepherd. In the valley of dry bones, YHWH sets Yehezkel down among bones that are very dry. Can these bones live? YHWH commands: Prophesy to these bones — and they come together, bone to bone, sinew and flesh cover them, and the breath enters them. YHWH says: These bones are the whole house of Yisra'EL — they say our bones are dried up, our hope is lost. But I will open your graves and bring you into the land. Two sticks — Yehudah and Efrayim — become one stick in YHWH's hand. Gog of the land of Magog comes against Yisra'EL — and YHWH destroys him with fire, brimstone, and pestilence.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the DSS Ezekiel fragments (4QEzek-a, 4QEzek-b, 4QEzek-c, 11QEzek) and the Orit Ge'ez. Chapter 34 — the denunciation of false shepherds — is the foundational prophetic critique of institutional leadership. Chapter 37 — the valley of dry bones — is the defining restoration vision of the entire prophetic literature. The bones are explicitly identified: 'these bones are the whole house of Yisra'EL' (37:11). The two-sticks prophecy (37:15-28) promises the reunification of the divided kingdoms — Yehudah and Efrayim/Yosef — into one nation under one shepherd. Chapters 38-39 — the Gog and Magog oracle — describe an eschatological invasion that YHWH himself defeats. The War Scroll at Qumran (1QM) draws on this framework for its eschatological battle scenario.

key_terms.definition: YHWH appoints Yehezkel as watchman over the house of Yisra'el: if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, the people's blood is on his hands; if he warns them and they do not listen, their blood is on their own heads. Yehezkel is personally responsible to deliver YHWH's word.

key_terms.term: YHWH Takes No Pleasure in the Death of the Wicked (Ezekiel 33:11)
key_terms.definition: YHWH declares: As I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Yisra'el? This restatement of the covenant appeal from Ezekiel 18 marks the transition from judgment oracles to restoration oracles.

On the day before a refugee arrived from Yerushalayim with the news of the city's fall, the hand of YHWH opened Yehezkel's mouth. When the refugee came and confirmed the fall, Yehezkel was no longer silent. His role shifts from judgment prophet to restoration prophet.

YHWH pronounces woe on the shepherds of Yisra'el who fed themselves instead of the flock: they ate the fat, clothed themselves with the wool, but did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, seek the lost, or bring back the strayed. YHWH will remove the shepherds from tending the flock and hold them accountable.

YHWH declares: Behold, I myself will search for my sheep and seek them out. I will gather them from the countries where they were scattered and bring them to their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Yisra'el, by the ravines. I will seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind up the injured, strengthen the weak.

YHWH will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep — those who ate and drank well but fouled the remaining water and pasture for others. YHWH will set over the restored flock his servant David as a shepherd and prince forever. YHWH will make a covenant of peace — a brit shalom — removing harmful beasts and causing blessing.

YHWH brought Yehezkel in the spirit to a valley full of bones — very dry. YHWH asked: can these bones live? Yehezkel prophesied as commanded. Bones came together, sinews and flesh came on them, skin covered them, and breath (ruakh) entered — a vast army stood on their feet. YHWH declares: I will bring you up from your graves and put my spirit (ruakh) in you, and you shall live.

YHWH commanded Yehezkel to take two sticks — one for Yehudah (Judah), one for Yosef/Efrayim (the northern kingdom) — and join them in his hand so they became one stick. YHWH declares: I will make them one nation in the land, one king over them. No longer two nations, no longer divided. YHWH's servant David will be king over them, and YHWH will make a brit shalom (covenant of peace) with them forever.

key_terms.term: Gog of the Land of Magog (Ezekiel 38-39)
key_terms.definition: YHWH's prophecy against Gog of the land of Magog, chief prince of Meshekh and Tuval: in the latter days, Gog will come against the restored Yisra'el dwelling securely. YHWH will bring Gog against the land as bait, then destroy him with earthquake, pestilence, blood, overflowing rain, hailstones, fire, and burning sulfur. All the nations will know that YHWH is YHWH.

key_terms.term: YHWH Will Restore His Spirit to Yisra'el (Ezekiel 39:29)
key_terms.definition: After the destruction of Gog and the full regathering of Yisra'el, YHWH declares: I will not hide my face anymore from them, when I pour out my spirit upon the house of Yisra'el. The covenant promise that drives the entire restoration section: YHWH's spirit poured out on the restored covenant people, never withdrawn again.

faq.question: What is the significance of the watchman responsibility assigned to Yehezkel?
faq.answer: YHWH's appointment of Yehezkel as watchman in Ezekiel 33 establishes personal prophetic accountability: the watchman's job is to warn, not to guarantee results. If Yehezkel delivers the warning and people ignore it, their blood is on their own heads; if he fails to warn, their blood is on his hands. This is a covenant accountability structure: YHWH uses human agents to deliver his covenant word, and those agents are personally responsible for faithful delivery. The watchman metaphor also implies a community responsibility — the people cannot say they were not warned.

faq.question: What is the indictment of the shepherds in Ezekiel 34 and who does it apply to?
faq.answer: YHWH's indictment of Yisra'el's shepherds in Ezekiel 34 applies to every kind of leadership — kings, priests, prophets, nobles — anyone entrusted with covenant community care. The failures catalogued are specific: feeding themselves at the community's expense, failing to strengthen the weak, failing to heal the sick, failing to seek the lost and strayed, using force against the flock. YHWH declares he will hold the shepherds accountable and remove them from tending the flock. The indictment is not abstract but describes the actual failure modes of Yehudah's leadership that led to the exile.

faq.question: What does YHWH mean by declaring himself the shepherd of Yisra'el in Ezekiel 34?
faq.answer: In Ezekiel 34:11-16, YHWH steps in as the shepherd who will do what the human shepherds failed to do: seek the scattered, bring back the strayed, bind the injured, strengthen the weak, feed them in good pasture. This is not simply a metaphor — it is a covenant declaration of YHWH's own direct action on behalf of the scattered exiles. YHWH will not leave the restoration to another human shepherd who might also fail. The language echoes Psalm 23 and the entire covenant tradition of YHWH as the one who provides, protects, and restores.

faq.question: What is the theological meaning of the valley of dry bones vision?
faq.answer: The valley of dry bones in Ezekiel 37 is YHWH's direct answer to the exiles' despair: Our bones are dried up, our hope is lost, we are cut off completely. YHWH demonstrates with the vision that there is no death from which YHWH cannot resurrect: bones — very dry, apparently beyond any hope — came together, received flesh and skin, and were given the ruakh (breath/spirit) of life. YHWH's explanation is explicit: the bones are the whole house of Yisra'el in exile. The restoration of the nation will be as miraculous as resurrection from death.

faq.question: What do the two sticks in Ezekiel 37 represent and why does the reunion matter?
faq.answer: The two sticks represent the divided kingdom: one stick for Yehudah (the southern kingdom, the exiles in Babylon), one stick for Yosef/Efrayim (the northern kingdom, scattered since 722 BCE). YHWH declares he will join them into one in his hand and make them one nation under one king — YHWH's servant David. The reunion matters because the division of the kingdom after Shlomo was itself a covenant consequence of Solomon's unfaithfulness, and the two-kingdom reality had persisted for centuries. The restoration YHWH promises is not just return from Babylon but complete covenant reunification of all twelve tribes.

faq.question: What is the brit shalom (covenant of peace) promised in Ezekiel 34 and 37?
faq.answer: YHWH's covenant of peace promised in Ezekiel 34:25 and 37:26 is the eschatological covenant that fulfills all the earlier covenant promises: YHWH will make a brit shalom with the restored people, remove harmful beasts from the land, cause the people to dwell securely, bless them with rain and agricultural abundance, multiply them, and place his sanctuary among them forever. YHWH's servant David will be their shepherd-king. The brit shalom is not a new covenant separate from Sinai but the fulfillment of the covenant promises that Yisra'el's unfaithfulness had delayed — now given without revocation.

faq.question: Who is Gog of Magog and what is the purpose of this prophecy?
faq.answer: Gog of Magog in Ezekiel 38-39 is a future coalition leader who will come against restored Yisra'el dwelling securely in the land. The prophecy does not specify a historical identity — it describes a final assault against the covenant community in the latter days. YHWH declares he will destroy Gog with earthquake, pestilence, fire, and brimstone, and all the nations will see that YHWH is YHWH. The purpose is not primarily about Gog but about the universal witness: YHWH's final act of covenant protection for the restored people will be visible to every nation and cannot be attributed to Yisra'el's own military power.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yehezkel's silence being broken when Yerushalayim fell?
faq.answer: In Ezekiel 24:27, YHWH told Yehezkel that on the day the Temple fell, his mouth would be opened. In Ezekiel 33:21-22, the night before a refugee arrived with news of the city's fall, YHWH opened Yehezkel's mouth. When the refugee confirmed the fall, Yehezkel was no longer mute. This marks the structural turning point of the entire book: before the fall, Yehezkel spoke primarily judgment oracles; after the fall, his ministry shifts to restoration prophecy. The silence was itself a sign — it ended when the judgment it had announced was confirmed.

faq.question: How does YHWH's promise to pour out his spirit in Ezekiel 39:29 connect to the restoration?
faq.answer: YHWH's promise in Ezekiel 39:29 — I will not hide my face anymore from them, when I pour out my spirit upon the house of Yisra'el — is the culminating covenant promise of the entire restoration section. Throughout the exile, YHWH had hidden his face because of the covenant violation. The pouring out of YHWH's ruakh (spirit) on the restored people is the reversal of everything that caused the exile: not just political return but covenant renewal, with YHWH's own presence dwelling in the people rather than withdrawn from them. This promise becomes the foundation for the vision of the restored Temple in Ezekiel 40-48.

faq.question: What is the brit shalom (covenant of peace) and how does it differ from the Sinai covenant?
faq.answer: In Ezekiel 34:25 and 37:26, YHWH promises a brit shalom — a covenant of peace — with the restored Yisra'el. This is not a replacement of the Sinai covenant but its eternal fulfillment: YHWH will make the covenant permanent, place his sanctuary among them forever, make them his people and be their Creator. The difference from Sinai is that this covenant comes after the full playing out of the exile consequences — after the judgment, after the purging, after the wilderness renewal. It is the same covenant obligations (Torah) now written in the heart (echoing Yirmeyahu 31), with YHWH's spirit poured out as the enabling power, and with YHWH's own sanctuary as the permanent dwelling rather than a portable Tabernacle.
